messages:
maria: quick question — running into a weird 401 when a long-lived Node streaming client crosses project boundaries. Setup: service account JWT we mint, exchange for OIDC access token, then open a streaming websocket/grpc. After switching the writable project in our UI (project A -> project B) the stream continues for a bit then we see repeated 401s and the server drops the stream. Anyone seen reauth + project scoping weirdness?

kevin: yep, seen this. Likely two issues: (1) the token you exchanged includes an audience/claim tied to project A (aud or custom claim) so server rejects it for project B, and (2) the Node SDK instance is caching the access token and not re-exchanging with the new project context.

sanjay: concrete workaround that helped our app: don't reuse the same client when switching projects if token audience changes. Either recreate the client or explicitly force a refresh before resuming streaming. Example (Node-ish):

```
// pseudo
await client.auth.getAccessToken({project: 'proj-B'}); // forces token exchange + cache update
const stream = client.openStream(...);
```

If you need to preserve connection, you have to push a new Authorization header into the stream metadata (see below).

ellen: adding a note about streaming protocols — gRPC doesn't let you atomically replace metadata for an existing bidi call in some runtimes. For websockets you can send an in-band "auth: refresh" control message that server understands and swaps token. For gRPC we implemented a short-lived control RPC to exchange an auth token pair without tearing down the heavy stateful stream.

maria: that's useful. Is there a recommended pattern for the SDK so app authors don't reinvent it? I can open a PR but want to align on preferred behavior.

kevin: recommended patterns (from smaller experiments):
- prefer server-side support for a lightweight token-refresh control message on streaming endpoints (most robust).
- client lib should expose a hook/option to provide a per-request token provider function rather than only a cached credential. e.g., `auth.getToken({context})` called on rotate interval.
- if audience/project changes, either recreate client or call `auth.invalidate()` then re-initiate stream.

sanjay: here's a sample token-provider pattern we added to our internal node SDK:

```
// register a token provider instead of static token
client.setTokenProvider(async (ctx) => {
  // ctx might include current project/route
  return await auth.exchangeServiceAccountForAccessToken({project: ctx.project});
});
// SDK uses provider() on refresh events and attaches returned bearer to metadata
```

This avoids global caching per client key and lets server-side project routing be correct.

ellen: small gotcha when using JWT->OIDC exchange: make sure the `aud` claim on the JWT matches the token endpoint expected audience. If you set `target_audience` or a custom aud, the resulting OIDC token might be invalid for the API's project check. In our case we had a middleware that injected `aud: https://token.example.com` which then made the final token unacceptable for project-scoped resource checks.

maria: thanks — that explains a lot. For our immediate fix I'll try forcing invalidate + re-open, and then follow up to add the provider callback. I'll open a draft PR.

kevin: ping me on the PR. Also consider surfacing a config flag `streamingAuth: {mode: 'provider'|'static', refreshWindow: 60}` so we can keep backwards compat.

maria: will do. drafting PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk/pull/5082 (DRAFT) — pinging @kevin @sanjay for early review :pray:

maria: noted, thanks all :heart:
